questions.clue: A distribution for an unknown parameter before updating with the current dataset.
questions.explanation: A prior expresses uncertainty about the parameter before the current observations enter the update.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 338, Prior distributions

questions.clue: The density or mass of the observed data, viewed as a function of an unknown parameter.
questions.explanation: Likelihood keeps the recorded data fixed while comparing parameter values.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 251, Likelihood

questions.clue: Each school has a different baseline taken from a shared distribution, with one common slope.
questions.explanation: The varying baseline is the school-specific intercept.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 354, Random effects model Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 5, Hierarchical models. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue: As sample size grows, an estimator converges in probability to the true parameter.
questions.explanation: A consistent estimator gets arbitrarily close to its target with probability approaching one.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 100, Consistency

questions.clue: A prior for a defect rate is updated with the results of 20 inspections. What is the updated distribution?
questions.explanation: The posterior summarizes uncertainty about the defect rate given the observed inspections.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 334, Posterior distributions

questions.clue: All eight hospitals share one fitted infection rate. What pooling strategy is used?
questions.explanation: One shared parameter treats all groups as having the same underlying rate.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 5, Hierarchical models. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue: After fitting, simulate full datasets from posterior draws and compare their medians with the observed median.
questions.explanation: The observed median is compared with medians from data generated under the fitted Bayesian model.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 334, Posterior predictive checks

questions.clue: An analyst chooses the rate parameter giving the observed counts their largest joint probability.
questions.explanation: Maximum likelihood estimation chooses the parameter value maximizing the likelihood.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 273, Maximum likelihood estimation

questions.clue:
Σᵢ log f(yᵢ∣θ)
Independent observations, fixed data.
questions.explanation: The logarithm turns the product of independent observations’ likelihood contributions into a sum.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 258, Log-likelihood

questions.clue:
p(θ)p(y∣θ) / p(y)
y is the observed data, θ the parameter.
choices: Likelihood as a function of θ
questions.explanation: Bayes’ rule normalizes the product of the prior and the likelihood by the marginal density of the data.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 39, Bayes’ Theorem Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 1, Probability and inference. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue:
θⱼ ∣ μ, τ ∼ Normal(μ, τ²)
θⱼ is the latent mean for group j. What is τ²?
questions.explanation: The group means vary around μ with conditional variance τ².
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 5, Hierarchical models. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue: P(∣Xₙ − X∣ > ε) → 0 for every ε > 0
questions.explanation: The probability of an error greater than any fixed tolerance goes to zero.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 104, Convergence in probability

questions.clue: Group estimates remain distinct while sharing information through an estimated common distribution.
questions.explanation: The shared distribution allows estimates from different groups to inform one another.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 5, Hierarchical models. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue: An interval contains 95% of the posterior mass for one unknown parameter.
choices: Prediction interval for a new datum
questions.explanation: Its posterior probability refers to the parameter given the observed data and the model.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 114, Credible region

questions.clue: Two responses are independent when the group effect is fixed. What property is stated?
questions.explanation: Conditioning fixes the shared effect. Marginalizing over that effect can make the responses dependent.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 5, Hierarchical models. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue: For each candidate value of the target parameter, maximize likelihood over all nuisance parameters.
questions.explanation: The nuisance parameters are optimized separately at each fixed value of the target.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 342, Profile likelihood

questions.clue: Xₙ converges in distribution to X. Which theorem gives exp(Xₙ) converging in distribution to exp(X)?
questions.explanation: The exponential is continuous, so applying it preserves convergence in distribution to the transformed limit.
questions.reference: Stanford STATS 200, Lecture 4, Asymptotics and simulation. https://web.stanford.edu/class/archive/stats/stats200/stats200.1172/Lecture04.pdf

questions.clue: Change the prior scale, keep the likelihood fixed, and compare posterior conclusions. What is this?
questions.explanation: Refitting with different priors shows whether conclusions depend on the prior specification.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 7, Evaluating, comparing, and expanding models. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 388, Sensitivity analysis

questions.clue: Temperature changes electricity use at a different fitted rate in each city. The rates follow a shared distribution.
questions.explanation: The slope is the change per unit of temperature, and this coefficient varies by city.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 5, Hierarchical models. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue: A researcher estimates each branch’s mean from that branch’s data alone, with independent fixed priors.
questions.explanation: With independent fixed priors and separate data, the group estimates borrow no information across branches.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 5, Hierarchical models. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue:
dℓ(θ)/dθ
ℓ is the log likelihood for fixed observations.
questions.explanation: The score is the first derivative of the log likelihood with respect to θ.
questions.reference: Stanford STATS 200, Lecture 14, Consistency and asymptotic normality of the MLE. https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats200/Lecture14.pdf

questions.clue: sqrt(n)(θ̂ₙ − θ) → in distribution to Normal(0, V), V > 0.
questions.explanation: The centered and scaled estimation error has a normal limiting distribution.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 23, Asymptotic distribution Stanford STATS 200, Lecture 14, Consistency and asymptotic normality of the MLE. https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats200/Lecture14.pdf

questions.clue:
∫ p(ỹ∣θ,y) p(θ∣y) dθ
y is observed, ỹ is one future outcome.
questions.explanation: Predictive uncertainty averages the conditional outcome density over the updated distribution for θ.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 1, Probability and inference. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf Ohio State STAT 6570, Spring 2024 syllabus, pp. 1–2, Course Learning Outcomes. https://stat.osu.edu/sites/default/files/2024-02/Spring%202024%20STAT%206570%20syllabus%20for%20insructor%20Chkrebtii.pdf

questions.clue:
Fₙ(x) → F(x) wherever F is continuous.
Fₙ and F are cumulative distribution functions.
questions.explanation: Agreement at all continuity points defines convergence in distribution.
questions.reference: Stanford STAT 208, Lectures, Notions of Convergence, Convergence in Law. https://web.stanford.edu/class/stat208/node3.html

questions.clue: A regular estimator attains the lowest limiting variance allowed by the model under the same scaling.
questions.explanation: Efficiency compares the large-sample precision of estimators using the same scaling.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 24, Asymptotic efficiency

questions.clue: Under a regular nested null, twice the maximized log-likelihood gain tends to χ² with degrees equal to the parameter-count difference.
questions.explanation: This gives the large-sample null reference distribution for the likelihood-ratio statistic.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 460, Wilks’ theorem
questions.convention: Assumes an interior true parameter and the standard regularity conditions.

questions.clue: A higher-level distribution is assigned to τ, the scale of a distribution for group effects. What is p(τ)?
questions.explanation: A hyperprior specifies uncertainty about a parameter of another prior distribution.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 211, Hyperprior

questions.clue: Combine model-specific predictions using each candidate’s posterior probability as its weight.
questions.explanation: The averaged prediction integrates uncertainty about which candidate model applies.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 38, Bayesian model averaging

questions.clue: A statistic tends in distribution to Z. Its random scale estimate tends in probability to c > 0. Which theorem gives the ratio limit Z/c?
questions.explanation: Slutsky’s theorem allows the estimated scale to be replaced by its nonzero probability limit in the ratio’s limit.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 399, Slutsky’s theorem Stanford STATS 200, Lecture 4, Asymptotics and simulation. https://web.stanford.edu/class/archive/stats/stats200/stats200.1172/Lecture04.pdf

questions.clue: The observed maximum exceeds nearly every replicated maximum. Which model feature does this check flag?
questions.explanation: The fitted model rarely generates a maximum as large as the one observed.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 334, Posterior predictive checks Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §6.3, Posterior predictive checking. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/bayescomputation/bdachapter6.pdf

questions.clue: Before fitting, draw rates from the prior and simulate outcomes to see if implausible counts are common.
questions.explanation: The simulation asks what data the joint prior and likelihood imply before conditioning on observations.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 6, Exercise 7, prior versus posterior predictive checks. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue: Predict outcomes at a hospital unseen during fitting by holding out each entire hospital in turn.
questions.explanation: Holding out whole groups assesses prediction for new groups instead of additional data from known groups.
questions.reference: Stan User’s Guide, Held-Out Evaluation and Cross-Validation, Cross-validation with structured data. https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_36/stan-users-guide/cross-validation.html

questions.clue:
Eθ[−ℓ″(θ)]
ℓ is the sample log likelihood, with expectation over the data.
questions.explanation: The expected negative curvature measures the information available about θ.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 167, Fisher’s information Stanford STATS 200, Lecture 14, Consistency and asymptotic normality of the MLE. https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats200/Lecture14.pdf
questions.convention: Assumes differentiability and the regularity conditions for the expected curvature identity.

questions.clue:
2(ℓ̂full − ℓ̂null)
Both log likelihoods are maximized under their respective nested models.
questions.explanation: The test statistic measures how much fit improves when the null restrictions are relaxed.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 251, Likelihood ratio test
questions.convention: Uses the common deviance scale, −2 times the log of the restricted/unrestricted likelihood ratio.

questions.clue:
p(y∣M₁) / p(y∣M₀)
Each model’s likelihood is integrated over its own prior.
choices: Posterior odds for M₁ vs M₀
Prior odds for M₁ vs M₀
Bayes factor for M₁ vs M₀
questions.answer: Bayes factor for M₁ vs M₀
questions.explanation: The ratio updates prior odds to posterior odds between the two models.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 37, Bayes factor

questions.clue: If sqrt(n)(θ̂ − θ) tends to N(0,V), the scaled error for g(θ̂) has limiting variance [g′(θ)]²V. Which method?
questions.explanation: A first-order expansion of g scales the limiting error by its derivative.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 128, Delta (δ) method
questions.convention: Assumes g is differentiable at θ with a nonzero derivative. N(mean, variance).

questions.clue: An analyst takes the ratio of two models’ probabilities after observing the data. What does that ratio give?
questions.explanation: Posterior odds equal prior odds multiplied by the Bayes factor.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 37, Bayes factor

questions.clue: A clinic model has one mean θⱼ for each clinic. At what level does θⱼ vary?
questions.explanation: Each θⱼ belongs to a particular clinic and is shared by observations within that clinic.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 5, Hierarchical models. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue: A Beta prior for a binomial probability gives another Beta distribution after updating. What property is illustrated?
questions.explanation: Conjugacy preserves the prior’s distribution family after updating with its matching likelihood.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 100, Conjugate prior

questions.clue: Which criterion uses posterior variance of pointwise log likelihoods as a penalty for predictive fit?
questions.explanation: The common WAIC form subtracts a pointwise posterior-variance penalty from the log predictive fit.
questions.reference: Gelman, Hwang and Vehtari, Understanding predictive information criteria for Bayesian models, §3.4, WAIC. https://stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/waic_understand3.pdf

questions.clue: An unknown parameter affects the likelihood but is outside the main inferential target.
questions.explanation: Inference must account for the unknown quantity even though the question targets something else.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 251, Likelihood

questions.clue: The distribution of possible observations before conditioning on any observed outcomes.
questions.explanation: The prior predictive averages possible outcomes over parameter values from the prior.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 6, Exercise 7, prior versus posterior predictive checks. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue: A test statistic has its reference distribution for every supported sample size.
questions.explanation: An exact reference distribution applies at finite sample sizes under the test assumptions.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 24, Asymptotic methods

questions.clue: In a model for many clinic effects, one shared parameter describes the center of their distribution.
questions.explanation: The center of the clinic-effect distribution is a population-level parameter.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §5.4, Estimating a normal population. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue: A scientist summarizes earlier lab results in a tightly concentrated distribution for a parameter before collecting new data.
questions.explanation: The prior concentrates probability using information available before the new experiment.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 218, Informative prior

questions.clue: For one dataset, an analyst divides the likelihood at one proposed parameter value by that at another. What is reported?
questions.explanation: The ratio compares how much the same observations support the two specified parameter values.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 244, Law of likelihood

questions.clue: A small school’s fitted effect moves from 12 to 8 after pooling toward a group-wide mean of 6. Where did it move?
questions.explanation: Partial pooling pulls a noisy estimate closer to the common center while allowing school differences.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §5.5, Estimating treatment effects in eight schools. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue: A model is scored on the same cases used to estimate every parameter. What kind of assessment is this?
questions.explanation: The score evaluates fit on the observations already seen during estimation.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 7, Evaluating, comparing, and expanding models. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue:
∏ᵢ f(yᵢ∣θ)
Data yᵢ are independent and held fixed. What function of θ is this?
questions.explanation: Independent observations contribute multiplicative terms to the likelihood.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 251, Likelihood

questions.clue:
−ℓ″(θ)
ℓ is the fixed-sample log likelihood and no expectation is taken.
questions.explanation: Observed information is the negative curvature of the log likelihood for the actual data.
questions.reference: Stanford STATS 364, Approximate likelihood and Bayesian methods (1), Fisher and observed information. https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats364/notebooks/Likelihood.html

questions.clue: arg max over θ of p(θ∣y)
questions.explanation: The maximum a posteriori estimate is a parameter value with highest posterior density or probability mass.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 272, Maximum a posteriori estimate (MAP)

questions.clue:
E[θ∣y]
Assume this expectation exists. Which posterior summary is it?
questions.explanation: A conditional expectation of the parameter given the data is its posterior mean.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 1, Probability and inference. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue: Relabeling the groups leaves the joint prior for their effects unchanged.
questions.explanation: Exchangeability means the joint distribution is invariant under permutation of labels.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 155, Exchangeability Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §5.2, Exchangeability. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue: Conditioning on this statistic makes the remaining data distribution independent of the unknown parameter.
questions.explanation: A sufficient statistic retains the information about the parameter contained in the sample.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 420, Sufficient statistic

questions.clue: A proposed prior density is proportional to a positive constant over the entire real line.
questions.explanation: The constant over an unbounded line cannot be normalized to integrate to one.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 213, Improper prior distribution

questions.clue: The estimator’s expected value tends to the true parameter as n grows. Which property follows directly?
questions.explanation: Asymptotic unbiasedness requires bias to tend to zero. It concerns expectations.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 23, Asymptotically unbiased estimator

questions.clue: A mean of i.i.d. readings converges in probability to the population mean. Which law gives this when the mean is finite?
questions.explanation: For independent identically distributed observations with a finite mean, the weak law gives this probability limit.
questions.reference: Stanford STATS 200, Lecture 4, Asymptotics and simulation. https://web.stanford.edu/class/archive/stats/stats200/stats200.1172/Lecture04.pdf

questions.clue: Let X be +1 or −1 with equal chance. Set Xₙ = −X for every n. How does Xₙ converge to X?
questions.explanation: The distributions match at every n, but the distance between Xₙ and X is always 2.
questions.reference: Stanford STAT 208, Lectures, Notions of Convergence, Convergence in Law. https://web.stanford.edu/class/stat208/node3.html

questions.clue: Estimate the shared prior scale from all groups, then condition on that single estimate for group-level inference.
questions.explanation: Estimating prior parameters from the data and plugging them in is an empirical Bayes strategy.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 150, Empirical Bayes method

questions.clue: Across many held-out cases, 67% fall within the supplied 90% predictive intervals. What pattern is evident?
questions.explanation: The observed fraction covered falls short of the advertised level on these test cases.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §7.1, Measures of predictive accuracy. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue:
ℓ′(θ̂) = 0
θ̂ is a differentiable interior maximum of the log likelihood. Which quantity is zero?
questions.explanation: At a differentiable interior maximum the first derivative vanishes.
questions.reference: Stanford STATS 200, Lecture 14, Consistency and asymptotic normality of the MLE. https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats200/Lecture14.pdf

questions.clue:
1 / sqrt[n I(θ̂)]
I is expected information per observation for a regular scalar model.
questions.explanation: Information adds across independent identically distributed observations. Taking the inverse square root gives a standard error.
questions.reference: Stanford STATS 200, Lecture 14, Consistency and asymptotic normality of the MLE. https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats200/Lecture14.pdf

questions.clue:
∫ p(y∣θ) p(θ) dθ
What is this function of y before observing it?
choices: Likelihood as a function of θ
questions.explanation: Averaging the observation model over the prior gives the prior predictive density.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 6, Exercise 7, prior versus posterior predictive checks. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue:
Yᵢⱼ ∣ θⱼ, σ ∼ Normal(θⱼ, σ²)
Groups vary through θⱼ. What does σ² represent?
choices: Variance of the group mean parameter
Variance of the grand mean parameter
questions.explanation: Holding the group mean fixed leaves the observation variance within its group.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §5.4, Estimating a normal population. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf

questions.clue: This test computes the score at the restricted null fit and scales it by information under the null.
questions.explanation: A score test asks whether the null fit has a large likelihood gradient in the direction of departure.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 383, Score test Stanford STATS 300B, Lecture 6, Testing: likelihood ratio, Wald, Score tests. https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats300b/syllabus.html

questions.clue: Two estimators have the same normal limit center and scaling. One has limiting variance 2 and the other 5. What favors the first?
questions.explanation: Under the same scaling, the smaller limiting variance gives a narrower large-sample distribution.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 24, Asymptotic efficiency

questions.clue: A 90% credible set includes only points whose posterior density is at least the density anywhere outside it.
questions.explanation: A highest-density set collects the most dense parameter values until reaching the required posterior mass.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 205, Highest posterior density region Lehmann and Romano, Testing Statistical Hypotheses, §5.7, Bayesian Confidence Sets. https://sites.stat.washington.edu/jaw/COURSES/580s/582/HO/Lehmann_and_Romano-TestingStatisticalHypotheses.pdf

questions.clue: What happens to information sharing if independent group effects have known common prior hyperparameters?
choices: Common prior targets, no group-to-group learning
Data in each group update the shared hyperparameters
Group estimates must all be identical
questions.answer: Common prior targets, no group-to-group learning
questions.explanation: With fixed hyperparameters and independent likelihoods, observations in other groups cannot update a group effect.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 5, Hierarchical models. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf
questions.convention: Assumes independent group effects given the fixed hyperparameters and independent likelihoods across groups.

questions.clue: To assess next-month forecasts, train on earlier months and repeatedly score the next available month.
questions.explanation: Keeping training before the forecast cutoff mimics the information available at deployment.
questions.reference: Stan User’s Guide, Held-Out Evaluation and Cross-Validation, Cross-validation with spatio-temporal data. https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_36/stan-users-guide/cross-validation.html

questions.clue: Want to simulate a new hospital, not more patients in observed hospitals. Which quantities must be generated anew?
questions.explanation: A replicate from a new hospital needs its own draw from the group-level distribution.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 7, Evaluating, comparing, and expanding models. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf Gelman, Hwang and Vehtari, Understanding predictive information criteria for Bayesian models, §2.5, Choices in defining the likelihood and predictive quantities. https://stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/waic_understand3.pdf

questions.clue: A count model looks good on the mean but may miss extra zeros. What statistic directly probes this issue?
questions.explanation: Replicated zero counts can be compared with the observed zero count to assess that specific mismatch.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §6.3, Posterior predictive checking. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/bayescomputation/bdachapter6.pdf

questions.clue: Two schools have identical raw scores. One estimate is based on five pupils, the other on 500. Which is pulled more toward the modeled mean?
choices: The school with the larger raw score
questions.explanation: A noisier group estimate gets less weight than a more precise one in a normal hierarchical model.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., §5.5, Estimating treatment effects in eight schools. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/BDA3.pdf
questions.convention: Assume otherwise equal conditions, including the same per-pupil variance and a positive between-school variance.

questions.clue:
Var(T) ≥ 1 / I(θ)
T is unbiased for θ, and I is sample Fisher information in a regular scalar model.
questions.explanation: The Cramér–Rao inequality bounds the variance of a regular unbiased estimator from below.
questions.reference: Stanford STATS 200, Lecture 15, Fisher information and the Cramér–Rao lower bound. https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats200/Lecture15.pdf

questions.clue:
[(θ̂ − θ₀) / SE(θ̂)]²
Use the unrestricted estimate and its estimated standard error.
questions.explanation: The Wald statistic measures the squared estimated distance from the null in standard-error units.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 451, Wald’s test Stanford STATS 300B, Lecture 6, Testing: likelihood ratio, Wald, Score tests. https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats300b/syllabus.html

questions.clue:
τ² / (τ² + σ²)
Independent random-intercept variance τ² and residual variance σ².
questions.explanation: Two distinct members of a group share the random intercept, which contributes their covariance.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 221, Intraclass correlation Penn State STAT 502, Lesson 6, Random Effects and Introduction to Mixed Models, intraclass correlation coefficient. https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat502/Lesson06

questions.clue:
Σᵢ log p(yᵢ∣y₋ᵢ)
Each i is left out when fitting the predictor for yᵢ.
questions.explanation: Every observation is scored using a predictive density conditioned on the remaining data.
questions.reference: Vehtari, Gelman and Gabry, Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC, expected log pointwise predictive density for leave-one-out cross-validation. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/research/published/loo_stan.pdf

questions.clue: The sequence converges pointwise on an event with probability one.
questions.explanation: Convergence almost surely concerns entire sample paths except on a probability-zero event.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 11, Almost sure convergence

questions.clue: Which posterior point summary minimizes expected absolute error for a scalar parameter?
questions.explanation: A posterior median balances posterior mass on either side and minimizes absolute loss.
questions.reference: Luc Demortier, Bayesian Statistics, Bayesian Point Estimation, absolute loss. https://hep-physics.rockefeller.edu/luc/talks/BayesianStatistics2013.pdf

questions.clue: An analyst uses posterior quantiles that leave the same probability below and above the interval. Which interval is this?
questions.explanation: The posterior probability excluded by the interval is split equally between the lower and upper tails.
questions.reference: Lehmann and Romano, Testing Statistical Hypotheses, §5.7, Bayesian Confidence Sets. https://sites.stat.washington.edu/jaw/COURSES/580s/582/HO/Lehmann_and_Romano-TestingStatisticalHypotheses.pdf

questions.clue: For a nested comparison, how does the unrestricted log-likelihood maximum compare with the restricted maximum?
questions.explanation: Every parameter value allowed by the restricted model is also available to the unrestricted fit.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 251, Likelihood ratio test

questions.clue: A first-order delta approximation gives variance zero at the target. What could yield a nondegenerate transformed limit?
choices: Replacing the sample size with one
questions.explanation: If the first derivative is zero, a higher-order term can determine the transformed statistic’s scaling and limit.
questions.reference: Stanford STATS 300B, Delta method, Higher-order delta methods. https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats300b/Slides/02-delta-method.pdf

questions.clue: Choose weights for combining models by maximizing the ensemble’s held-out log predictive performance.
choices: Bayesian model averaging by posterior odds
questions.explanation: Stacking optimizes weights for the combined predictive distribution using out-of-sample scores.
questions.reference: Yao et al., Using Stacking to Average Bayesian Predictive Distributions, stacking of predictive distributions. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/research/published/stacking.pdf

questions.clue:
p ∼ Dirichlet(α) and X ∣ p ∼ Multinomial(n, p).
Which family contains p’s posterior?
questions.explanation: The Dirichlet prior is conjugate for the multinomial probabilities. Observed category counts update its parameters.
questions.reference: UC Berkeley STAT 238, Lecture Thirteen, Dirichlet Prior and Multinomial Likelihood. https://stat238.berkeley.edu/spring-2026/lecturethirteen238spring2026/

questions.clue: For any ε > 0, some finite M satisfies supₙ P(∣Zₙ∣ > M) < ε. What property does this define?
questions.explanation: A single bounded interval can contain arbitrarily high probability for every distribution in the sequence.
questions.reference: Stanford STATS 300B, Lecture 14, Tightness, Definitions 0.1–0.2 and Theorem 2. https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats300b/ScribeNotes/2021/lecture-14.pdf
